## Marketing Against the Grain — 📸  Your camera doesn’t matter

_From: `[email]` · 2026-06-01T02:05:05+00:00_

Here’s 3 things to obsess over instead before your next video ad

View in browser (https://marketingagainstthegrain.com/your-camera-doesnt-matter?ecid=ACsprvvtUTT2XDWiGyJyOdNtwKECjGjNbCZVYXgoaC_kmPVBsz0tk-Sd0cxBjWNn3sI7TybxiMCG&_hsenc=p2ANqtz--HsWNL3Xn5nS0H5z5xpR4c7yX9Kkft3EY-K0i-rwi-U8G5gp6sb5zdGnW3MxQeTDYNmkoJ98FwKRAcR1KtJ90rLBZEAg&_hsmi=421477525 )

June 1, 2026

Marketing Against the Grain (https://marketingagainstthegrain.com/?_hsenc=p2ANqtz--HsWNL3Xn5nS0H5z5xpR4c7yX9Kkft3EY-K0i-rwi-U8G5gp6sb5zdGnW3MxQeTDYNmkoJ98FwKRAcR1KtJ90rLBZEAg&_hsmi=421477525 )

Where most marketers pad, Grace Wells deletes.

She’s built a following of nearly 4 million across channels, and she did it by mastering a skill that too many of us ignore — knowing when to stop.

Meet the Master

Grace Wells

Commercial video creator and Founder, Product Film School (https://productfilmschool.com/?_hsenc=p2ANqtz--HsWNL3Xn5nS0H5z5xpR4c7yX9Kkft3EY-K0i-rwi-U8G5gp6sb5zdGnW3MxQeTDYNmkoJ98FwKRAcR1KtJ90rLBZEAg&_hsmi=421477525 )

-

Fun fact: She produced an ad for a major pharmaceutical company for less than your company’s last offsite — under $10k! — and it ran on TV for over a year.

Lesson 1:

Trim the fat.

Even if you don’t know Grace Wells by name, you probably know her from her signature video intros.

“The way that I introduce all my videos is by reading a comment, and then I'll cut mid-sentence into the meat of what I'm doing behind the scenes,” Wells explains.

Of course, it took time to establish that. But now, she says, “the audience knows where I’m going with this. I don't even need to finish this sentence before I jump into the next shot.”

“That’s taught me that as soon as you’ve reached the moment where the audience understands the purpose of this shot, or this line of dialogue, or this piece of copy — as soon as there’s that recognition and understanding — you move on right away and don’t linger on anything.”

Lesson 2:

Your camera is the least important thing on set.

In 2024, Wells launched Product Film School to teach budding video creators what she’s learned about product advertising on a budget. “Creators will often prioritize the wrong things,” she tells me. “Like, people place way too much emphasis on what camera to use.”

And that’s actually not as important as you might think. Even Olivia Rodrigo shot a music video on an iPhone 15 Pro (“get him back!”, and it’s a banger).

“The bigger priority is making sure that you have really great lighting,” Wells says. “That is the make-it-or-break-it thing for me.”

If you want to get really granular, think about “creating depth and contrast in a shot,” she suggests. “Make sure that you have light sources that point at the product not just from the front, but also the back, so you’re creating a separation from the background.”

Lighting and storytelling are not things that require budget. They are really just foundational skills that you can cultivate to help you produce really great content.

In her Product Film School, Wells also emphasizes the importance of having a point of view, even for a short product video. What you’re creating has to actually say something, she says, even if it’s a 6-second looping reel. ”You can have that visual piece where you're making the product look really beautiful, but if you're not saying anything, then that content is going to fall flat.”

Lean on your narrative devices, Wells says. Maybe the video shows how a product solves a particular problem. “Or maybe we present the product as a sort of enigma at the beginning of the video — there’s a mystery to uncover about the product and then we solve that mystery.”

“Lighting and storytelling are not things that require budget. They are really just foundational skills that you can cultivate to help you produce really great content, even if it’s just with a couple of lights, a backdrop, and a few props from Michael’s.”

Lesson 3:

Make your ad look like it already lives there.

Wells tells me about a piece of content she created for a wellness brand with a very nature-inspired aesthetic. Normally, she says, you’d expect elements like neutral colors and other things that convey tranquility and calm.

But the internet is anything but tranquil and calm.

So Wells took the wellness blueprint and added visual digital elements that Instagram or TikTok users might expect — “we had cursors moving through the frame and hovering over the product, a pop-up that shows the brand and a messaging point,” and other elements that felt native to online platforms.

“Anything that you can do to integrate the infrastructure of the platform will make it feel more organic to the world in which people are watching it,” Wells explains. “It’s part of the fabric of your feed as opposed to this cutaway.”

Next time you’re scripting a social ad, ask yourself what that platform’s furniture looks like — and borrow some of it for a lived-in, organic feel.

Bryce Rattner Keithley [ https://substack.com/redirect/e2e7db5f-16ed-47cb-80f4-f34a667a8664?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] spent her career in talent and recruiting and had never written a line of code. Then she used AI to build Daily Hundred, a fitness app with custom AI-generated videos of animals doing exercises, and shipped it to the App Store. In this episode, Bryce shares the exact workflow she used with Replit, Claude, Gemini, Higgsfield, and Kling; why being non-technical became an advantage; and what her journey reveals about how AI is changing who gets to build software.
Biggest takeaways:
You can build and ship a production iPhone app with zero technical background. Bryce spent her entire career in talent and recruiting, had never written code, and still managed to build Daily Hundred—a fitness app with custom AI-generated videos—and get it approved in the App Store. The entire process took a few months of weekend work.
The workflow that worked: Claude as architect, Claude Code as engineer, Terminal as executor. Bryce used regular Claude as her “friend in the cockpit” to plan what to do and how to approach problems. Claude would tell her when to use Claude Code to write actual code. She’d bring the code back to Claude for confirmation, then Claude would tell her what to paste into Terminal. This three-step dance—plan, execute, deploy—let her ship production code without having to know exactly how it all worked.
Screenshots and iteration are your best debugging tools. When AI wasn’t understanding what Bryce wanted, she’d either get more literal in her descriptions, completely restart the prompt (not just edit it), or send screenshots showing what she was seeing. Sometimes she’d even draw what she wanted or photograph her own starting position to give the AI a visual reference. The key was trying different approaches rather than getting stuck in one failed pattern.
The role of technical expertise is fundamentally changing. Bryce observed that engineers who come into technical interviews focused only on finding a working solution fastest are missing the point—“the robots can find a working solution faster than they can.” The human role has shifted to something broader: understanding the full suite of tools, knowing when to use AI versus when to step in personally, and bringing taste and judgment to the process. What got people here won’t get them there [ https://substack.com/redirect/525b13db-39ac-4562-9f51-b4fbf32d7d4f?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ].
Hiring for adaptability and openness matters more than ever. In Bryce’s view, people who get territorial about what they used to do or what other people used to do will struggle with relevance. The winners will be those with “the humility and the curiosity to work with others in ways that you haven’t before” and who recognize that “people can contribute in ways that they haven’t before.” The best idea should win, regardless of where it comes from.

# ‘Backrooms’ and ‘Obsession’ Break Box Office Records

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/8551c73b-c239-4cf9-be25-2f4a83aacf05/0601_Article_Photo_1.png?t=1780328319)
Caption: (Left to right) Kane Parsons and Curry Barker's films top the weekend fox office and Markiplier releases his on YouTube / [A24](https://www.instagram.com/p/DYFZ19mkSCt/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&igsh=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==), [Obsession](https://www.instagram.com/p/DYPghnbGxVH/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&igsh=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==), and photography by Jesse Leon

This weekend felt like a [pivotal moment](https://www.imdb.com/chart/boxoffice/) for creators in Hollywood—the top two films at the global box office were directed by YouTube creators. 

* Kane Parsons’ _Backrooms_ broke the record for largest opening weekend for an original horror movie, grossing $118M. It makes Parsons the youngest filmmaker ever to top the box office and was A24’s largest opening ever. 

* Comedy creator Curry Barker’s _Obsession_ has grossed $148M worldwide so far, on track to become one of the most profitable films of all time. 

* And Markiplier’s _Iron Lung_ raked in $52M globally before it was [released on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TQqav0_fbdk) for rent and purchase yesterday.

**Creator POV: **“I don't think there's that much of a difference from a technical perspective of making a movie versus a YouTube video,” Markiplier said on stage at Press Publish LA last week. “It's just the scale at which it is done.”

What do these creator-filmmakers have in common? Enormous success. But the different routes they all took to get there illustrate the diversity that makes this creator niche so unique.

**Here’s the breakdown, by the numbers →**

__**Backrooms**__
**Cost:** $10M
**How it was made:** Adapted from Parsons’ short film series as a co-production between A24, 21 Laps, Chernin Entertainment, and Blumhouse-Atomic Monster
**Distribution:** A24 distributed to over 3,400 theaters in North America (with more globally)

__**Iron Lung**__
**Cost: **Just under $5M
**How it was made:** Markiplier self-financed, wrote, directed, produced, and starred in the film
**Distribution:** Film distribution company Centurion distributed to over 4,600 theaters worldwide

__**Obsession**__
**Cost:** $750K
**How it was made:** Production company Blumhouse-Atomic Monster picked up Barker’s original script, shooting it in 20 days
**Distribution:** Focus Features picked up the rights to the film at TIFF in 2025 and distributed to over 2,000 theaters globally

**What does this mean for creators?** They’re getting audiences to show up, and Hollywood is noticing. Gen Z (the largest demographic for all three films) is flocking to the theater to see creators they already know try new media based on original IP. Filmmaker Mark Duplass (who has a role in _Backrooms_) said these wins are a "glimmer of hope" in a fractured distribution landscape. 

“We’ve got examples of creators woodshedding things, putting them online, building an audience, and now the people with the purse strings are going to notice,” Duplass said [on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/DY-KPcdJxYP/).

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/2e5fb3a9-11d3-45f1-967e-8eca4950d0e8/25-0121_Divider-Full_Logo-Grey.png?t=1769186993)
Caption: 

# What Brands Want from YouTube Creators

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/dc9e7bef-3661-4891-9a7e-a4e920f7d7f4/0601_Article_Photo_2.png?t=1780328361)
Caption: YouTube VP of Partnerships for the Americas Tim Katz (right) speak with Colin (left) and Samir (second from left) onstage at Press Publish LA / Photography by Jesse Leon

YouTube recently shared that it has _15 different ways_ for creators to monetize. At Press Publish LA last week, YouTube VP of Partnerships for the Americas [Tim Katz](https://www.linkedin.com/in/tim-katz-bb89867/) joined Colin and Samir [onstage](https://www.instagram.com/reels/DY5MNdiRjDY/) to talk through what the new options mean for creators—and what brands expect as a result.

**Katz's POV:** Brands want two things—_return on ad spend_ and _brand relevancy_. 

“Your viewers know when something isn't authentic to who you are,” Katz said. “The needle to thread for creators is, ‘How do you bring your audience in and bring that relevancy to the brand, but at the same time do it in a way that's actually authentic?’”

**Why brands want higher collaboration:** As audiences spend more time watching YouTube on TV, and YouTubers are making more content that feels like TV shows. Brands, according to Katz, want to feel integrated into the narrative of the show instead of a “30-second pre-roll.” 

This can happen in two ways: 

1. Backing a creator on their own channel to make a larger-than-life show, like Michelle Khare’s [7 Marathons series](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3zDt-QeJIw4) sponsored by Red Bull.

2. Producing a creator-led series on the brand’s own channel, like [Cadillac’s F1 series](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FLK9a0BPjcI&t=62s).

**Supporting these projects: **Katz shared that YouTube is improving TV playlist features so creators can lay out their channels into episodes, seasons, and series—mimicking traditional streaming services like Netflix.

“We're trying to make sure that the user experiences are matching the creator ambitions and the advertiser ambitions, and that it all syncs up together,” Katz said.

## @benradack
The reason your account always crashes the week after a big sale and how to prevent it.

During a promo, everything looks amazing. Your warm audience floods in to grab the deal.

Then the sale ends and the account falls off a cliff.

How to prevent it.

→ Keep your evergreen campaigns running alongside the promo. Don't pause them.

→ Ramp up creative testing during the sale. The promo carries your CPA so you can afford to test aggressively.

→ Batch test 30-50 new evergreen ads while the promo runs.

→ Walk out of the sale with 5-10 new proven winners ready to catch the account when the discount ends.

The week after a sale is won or lost during the sale. Not after it.

Prepare while the promo is carrying you. Not when it's already over.

## @benradack
Here are a few things I did that lowered my client's CPA by 47%.

→ **Launched over 100 ads**

Took all 100, put them in one CBO, and broke them out by customer profile into individual ad sets (around 30 each). 

Helped find winners fast. Probably missed a few but the speed was worth it.

→ **Lowered the cost cap**

Sounds dumb but the old campaign was running on fatigued ads with high CPAs. I lowered the cost cap by around 30% and it brought things down nicely. The old campaign barely spends anything now, but since the new one is doing so well, it all works together.

→ **New landing pages**

This part I can't take credit for. My client has a killer strategist running things and he implemented a great new LP. 

My only part here was making sure I coordinated with him to use the right LP for each offer. Good organizational skills as a media buyer go a long way.

This definitely helped bring the CPA down.

Sometimes it's not one big change. It's a few moves working together at the same time.

## @heyitsalexp
Speaking of "scaling DNA"...

...there's this clothing brand called Brandy Melville. They literally only sell ONE size: a women's 0/2

Took a category with major inventory risk and huge return rates driven by fit issues, and dramatically reduced those costs in one move.

Was this controversial? Hell yeah.

The "category convention" in apparel is that, by restricting yourself to a single size, you're losing out on a huge portion of the market.

And by choosing 0/2 as your size, you're going to attract a lot of negative consumer sentiment. 

Brandy Melville did it anyway. The brand has grown steadily, profitably 20-30% YoY for the past ~10 years.

The retail stores are always packed–teens and women in their early 20s love the brand, because it delivers high(er) quality, stylish clothing in 100% natural fibers at fast fashion prices (ex. $35 for a 100% cotton dress).

Yes, the sizing has caused controversy...but the brand kept growing. 

The moral of the story: to get something that most brands don't have (steady, profitable growth), you have to do something that most of your competitors are not willing to do.

That often means doing something that shatters "category conventions"–something that would make the "legacy" players think you are nuts.
